lesson.title: Route 66 and the Search for Work
lesson.summary: As Dust Bowl farms failed and banks foreclosed through the 1930s, hundreds of thousands of families from Oklahoma and neighboring states migrated west along Route 66 to California, hoping to find farm work, though many found poverty and discrimination instead of the better life they had been promised.
lesson.body:
The collapse of farming across the southern plains left many families with no land, no crop, and no income. Beginning in the early 1930s and continuing through the decade, hundreds of thousands of people loaded whatever belongings would fit into cars and trucks and headed west on Route 66 toward California, drawn by handbills and rumors of plentiful farm work in the state's fertile valleys. Because so many came from Oklahoma, the migrants were widely labeled Okies, even though many actually came from Texas, Arkansas, Missouri, and Kansas. The term was often used as an insult by Californians who saw the newcomers as a burden.

The reality that greeted the migrants rarely matched the promise. California's Central Valley did need seasonal farm labor, but far more workers arrived than there were jobs, which drove wages down and left growers with the upper hand. Many families ended up in makeshift roadside camps or grower-owned labor camps with little sanitation, moving from harvest to harvest picking cotton, grapes, or fruit for whatever wages they could get. Some California officials responded with hostility rather than help. In 1936, Los Angeles police officers were sent to state border crossings in an episode known as the bum blockade, turning away migrants they judged likely to need public assistance, before the effort was abandoned as illegal.

The migration became one of the most documented human stories of the Depression. Photographer Dorothea Lange, working for a federal relief agency, captured images such as Migrant Mother in 1936 that put a face on the crisis for the rest of the country. John Steinbeck's 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath followed a fictional Oklahoma family, the Joads, on the same journey and brought national attention, and no small amount of controversy, to the conditions migrants faced. The federal Farm Security Administration built camps, including one in Arvin, California, often called the Weedpatch Camp, that offered migrant families cleaner housing and basic services than the private camps did.

The Okies migration reshaped California's Central Valley and its agricultural workforce, and the hardships migrants organized against, low pay, unsafe conditions, and a lack of legal protection, fed directly into the farm labor organizing that would continue in California for decades afterward.
